blogs.title: Defining 'Intrinsic' Acts: The Eighth Circuit Tightens the Net Around Prior Possession Testimony
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Eighth Circuit's reaffirmation of *United States v. Battle* regarding the admissibility of prior firearm possession as 'intrinsic evidence.' The article examines how courts distinguish between impermissible character evidence under Rule 404(b) and proof of continuous possession essential to establishing the elements of a felon-in-possession charge. By upholding testimony that witnesses saw the specific sawed-off rifle 'a handful of times' prior to the incident, the opinion clarifies that continuity of control is often a matter of fact rather than prohibited propensity, offering critical guidance for prosecutors building cases where physical recovery occurs days or weeks after the initial crime.

blogs.title: Beyond ACAs: Navigating the Tension Between Mandatory Minimums and § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) Enhancements
blogs.description: Focusing on the sentencing phase, this piece dissects the interaction between the Armed Career Criminal Act (ACCA) mandatory minimums and the Four-Level Enhancement for possessing a firearm in connection with another felony under USSG § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B). While ACCA sets a statutory floor, this blog explores how appellate courts handle defendants who argue that applying additional guideline enhancements—even those leading to sentences already within ranges—violates the 'necessary' requirement of 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a). The analysis highlights *Cutbank*'s rejection of the argument that overlapping statutory and guideline punishments create redundancy, reinforcing that distinct aggravating conduct justifies separate sentencing considerations even when a mandatory minimum is triggered.

blogs.title: Procedural Minimalism at Sentencing: What *Cutbank* Says About Judicial Consideration of § 3553(a)
blogs.description: This post investigates the Eighth Circuit's reliance on recent precedents (*Masood*, *Maluoth*) to affirm sentences based on a presumption that district courts considered all relevant factors without needing a 'mechanical recitation.' The article critiques this trend toward procedural minimalism, questioning whether high-volume dockets are eroding meaningful judicial engagement with mitigation arguments. Using *Cutbank*'s complex background—including domestic violence, kidnapping, and resistance against law enforcement—as a case study, it evaluates when an appellate court might find that silence on specific mitigators constitutes reversible error versus when it merely reflects a judge's exercise of discretion within a well-documented record.
